content: Laparoscopic colposuspension is one of the earliest minimally invasive surgical techniques developed to treat stress urinary incontinence in women. It was initially thought to offer benefits such as shorter hospital stays and faster recovery times compared to traditional open surgery. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of laparoscopic colposuspension for urinary incontinence and to summarize findings from economic evaluations of this intervention. The review included 26 randomized controlled trials involving a total of 2,271 women. Thirteen trials compared laparoscopic colposuspension to open colposuspension, while nine trials compared it to midurethral sling procedures. One trial compared laparoscopic colposuspension using one suture versus two sutures, and three trials compared laparoscopic colposuspension using sutures versus mesh and staples. Most studies had follow-up periods of less than 18 months, and the overall risk of bias was unclear for selection, performance, and detection, but low for attrition and reporting. When comparing laparoscopic colposuspension using sutures to open colposuspension, there was little difference in subjective cure rates within 18 months (risk ratio [RR] 1.04, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.99 to 1.08; high-quality evidence). However, the evidence was very low quality when comparing laparoscopic colposuspension using mesh and staples to open colposuspension, making it uncertain whether one approach is superior for subjective cure (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.93). The risk of requiring repeat continence surgery after laparoscopic colposuspension remains unclear. Laparoscopic colposuspension may have a lower risk of perioperative complications compared to open colposuspension (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.94; low-quality evidence). However, there may be similar or higher rates of bladder perforations with laparoscopic colposuspension (RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.90 to 3.29; moderate-quality evidence). Rates of de novo detrusor overactivity (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.72 to 2.30) and voiding dysfunction (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.31) appear to be similar between the two approaches, but the evidence is uncertain due to wide confidence intervals. Quality of life outcomes were reported in five studies, but the data could not be synthesized. When comparing laparoscopic colposuspension using sutures to tension-free vaginal tape (TVT), there was little difference in subjective cure rates within 18 months (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.16; low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was little difference between laparoscopic colposuspension using mesh and staples and TVT (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.91; low-quality evidence). For laparoscopic colposuspension compared to midurethral slings, there may be lower rates of repeat continence surgery (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.04 to 3.62; low-quality evidence) and similar risks of perioperative complications (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.64; low-quality evidence), but the evidence is uncertain due to wide confidence intervals. De novo detrusor overactivity (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.88) and voiding dysfunction (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.47 to 2.41) rates were also similar, but the evidence remains uncertain. No studies reported on bladder perforations in this comparison. In the comparison of one suture versus two sutures in laparoscopic colposuspension, subjective cure rates within 18 months may be higher with two sutures (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.64; low-quality evidence). One suture may have lower rates of repeat continence surgery (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.37) and similar risks of perioperative complications (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.70), but the evidence is uncertain due to wide confidence intervals. Voiding dysfunction rates may be higher with one suture compared to two sutures (RR 2.82, 95% CI 0.30 to 26.54; low-quality evidence), but again, the evidence is uncertain. This trial did not report on bladder perforations, de novo detrusor overactivity, or quality of life. When comparing laparoscopic colposuspension using sutures to mesh and staples, it is uncertain whether one approach is better for subjective cure within 18 months (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.59; very low-quality evidence). The risk of repeat continence surgery was also uncertain (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.06 to 14.91; very low-quality evidence). However, laparoscopic colposuspension with sutures may increase the risk of perioperative complications compared to mesh and staples (RR 1.94, 95% CI 1.09 to 3.48; low-quality evidence). Rates of de novo detrusor overactivity may be similar (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.17 to 3.06; low-quality evidence), but the evidence is uncertain. None of the studies reported on bladder perforations, voiding dysfunction, or quality of life. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that there is likely little difference in subjective cure rates within 18 months between laparoscopic colposuspension and open colposuspension, or between laparoscopic colposuspension and midurethral sling procedures. However, much of the evidence is of low quality, leaving significant uncertainty about the effectiveness and safety of laparoscopic colposuspension. Future research should include larger trials with long-term follow-up and focus on clinically important outcomes. Three economic evaluations were identified, but they were not quality-assessed and should be interpreted cautiously in light of the clinical findings.
